If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis

Details: The test `testPropertyOptionGroup` sets up two mutually exclusive option groups (group1 with options "a" and "b", and group2 with options "x" and "y"). It simulates command line input with option "-a" and default properties also specifying options "b" and "x". Because "a" and "b" are mutually exclusive options in the same OptionGroup, logically, only one should be selected, and the parser should throw an error or reject the default option "b" since "-a" is specified on the command line.

Inspecting the `Parser.parse` method shows that it first processes command line arguments by iterating over tokens and invoking `processOption` for options. This `processOption` method calls `updateRequiredOptions(opt)` and adds the option to the command line. Notably, `processOption` uses cloned `Option` objects and throws an `UnrecognizedOptionException` for unknown options.

After processing the command line options, the parser then calls `processProperties(properties)` in `parse` to add options from default properties that were not present in the command line. In `processProperties`, for each default property option not already in the command line, the code fetches the corresponding option and sets its value, if it has arguments. For options without arguments, it only adds them if the property value is one of "yes", "true", or "1". Then, `cmd.addOption(opt)` is called, and `updateRequiredOptions(opt)` is also invoked here.

The key problem is in `processProperties`: the code adds default options directly to the command line without checking or updating the state of the respective `OptionGroup`. Specifically, `processProperties` does not check for mutual exclusivity violations in `OptionGroup`, unlike `processOption` which calls `updateRequiredOptions(opt)`. The code comment hints at this ("if the option is part of a group, check if another option of the group has been selected"), but no such check is implemented. The `OptionGroup.setSelected` method throws `AlreadySelectedException` if conflicting options are selected, but this mechanism is not invoked for default options.

Therefore, when the test passes "-a" on command line and sets "b" = "true" in properties, both "a" and "b" end up in the resulting CommandLine object without conflict detection. This violates mutually exclusivity and explains the test failure.

The recent reports also note related issues where default options are not correctly accounted for when checking required options, which aligns with the general theme of default options not being fully processed.

In summary, the bug is that the parser does not properly check or update OptionGroup selection state for default options loaded from Properties, allowing mutually exclusive options to coexist without error.

Suggested fix: The parser's `processProperties` method should be updated to check and update the state of any OptionGroup that the default option belongs to. This can be done by invoking the `OptionGroup.setSelected` method for that option and handling possible `AlreadySelectedException` just like in `processOption`.

This would enforce mutual exclusivity among default options and between command line and default options consistently.

Methods involved:
- `Parser.parse(Options, String[], Properties, boolean)`
- `Parser.processProperties(Properties)`
- `Parser.processOption(String, ListIterator)`
- `OptionGroup.setSelected(Option)`

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
